study_identification_part.si4_title: Hippocampal-amygdalo-ventricular atrophy score: Alzheimer disease detection using normative and pathological lifespan models

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To develop an innovative MRI-based method for Alzheimer disease (AD) detection and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) prognosis using lifespan trajectories of brain structures. The study proposes a novel Hippocampal-Amygdalo-Ventricular Atrophy score (HAVAs) based on both normative lifespan models and AD lifespan models.

Classification based on which model (CN or AD) is closest; HAVAs > 50% indicates closer to AD model. For normative modeling comparison, 2σ threshold used to detect abnormal values.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: The study used multiple approaches for association analysis: (1) For diagnostic classification (AD vs CN), performance was evaluated using balanced accuracy (BACC), specificity (SPE), sensitivity (SEN), and area under the ROC curve (AUC) based on HAVAs scores. (2) For prognostic classification (sMCI vs pMCI), the same metrics were used. (3) Comparisons were made with: normative modeling approaches (single structures and HAV combination using 2σ threshold), classical ML methods (SVM with RBF kernel, LASSO logistic regression with default Matlab parameters), and deep learning methods (ROI-based CNN, subject-based CNN, patch-based CNN from ClinicaDL/Wen et al. 2020). (4) Model selection on training data used screening of 33 structures that showed significant divergence between CN and AD models (non-overlapping confidence intervals) to identify most discriminant structures based on classification accuracy on training ADNI dataset. (5) Statistical validation of polynomial models included F-statistic (ANOVA), T-statistic for coefficients, and BIC for model selection, all with significance thresholds p < 0.05.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: HAVAs achieved highly accurate AD detection (AUC ≥94% on external datasets AIBL and MIRIAD) and good MCI prognosis (AUC=78% for sMCI vs pMCI discrimination), outperforming normative modeling, classical ML, and recent deep learning methods.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study demonstrated that the HAVAs score (combining hippocampus + amygdala - inferior lateral ventricle volumes) achieved superior classification performance compared to single-structure models and state-of-the-art methods. For diagnostic tasks: on AIBL (467 CN/82 AD), HAVAs achieved 88% BACC and 94% AUC; on MIRIAD (23 CN/46 AD), it achieved 89% BACC and 96% AUC. For prognostic task on ADNI-MCI (255 sMCI/235 pMCI), HAVAs achieved 73% BACC and 78% AUC despite being trained only on AD and CN subjects. HAVAs outperformed the second-best methods by 3 percentage points for both diagnosis and prognosis. Compared to individual structures, amygdala was the most discriminant single structure (BACC 80-88% for diagnosis), followed by hippocampus (74-80%), and inferior lateral ventricle (79-86%). The multimodel approach consistently outperformed single-model normative modeling: HAVAs (88% BACC on AIBL) vs. Normative HAV model (81%) vs. Normative hippocampus model (70%). HAVAs also performed better than CNN-based deep learning methods from Wen et al. 2020: ROI-based CNN (84% BACC on AIBL), subject-based CNN (83%), and patch-based CNN (81%). Classical ML methods using HAV structures showed intermediate performance: LASSO HAV (85%), SVM HAV (82%). Sensitivity analysis using different training datasets (AIBL, OASIS, MIRIAD) and testing on ADNI confirmed robustness: 87% BACC and 93% AUC, demonstrating good generalization and stability to training domain selection.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study introduced several innovations: (1) Screening approach: systematic analysis of 132 structures, 5 lobes, 4 regional tissues, and 3 tissues to identify the 33 structures showing significant divergence between CN and AD models, then screening for the most discriminant structures. (2) Volume normalization strategy: ICV normalization followed by z-score standardization using mean/SD from all CN subjects, enabling combination of structures with different sizes without hyperparameters. (3) Dual-model framework: using both CN and AD lifespan trajectories for classification, rather than single normative model, providing pathology-specific decision boundary. (4) Novel HAVAs score: probability-based continuous score (0-100%) rather than binary classification, computed from Euclidean distances to both models, normalized so scores sum to 1. (5) Age-dependent scoring: incorporating the distance δ between models as a function of age into the scoring formula. (6) Clinical interpretability: emphasis on simplicity and interpretability - method is fully understandable (hippocampal-amygdalo atrophy and ventricular enlargement) and uses fewer than 10 parameters compared to millions in CNN models. (7) Software availability: will be made available through volBrain platform (http://www.volbrain.net/) and as downloadable Docker (https://github.com/volBrain/AssemblyNetAD).

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This paper is notable for proposing a dual-model normative approach (both CN and AD trajectories) rather than traditional single-model normative modeling. The final HAVAs model is based on only three structures (hippocampus, amygdala, inferior lateral ventricle) selected from a comprehensive screening of 140 brain regions. The study trained models using N=2,655 CN subjects (age range 0.74-94 years) and N=2,251 subjects for AD trajectories (377 AD patients aged 55-96 years + 1,874 CN subjects younger than 55 years). The approach assumes that neurodegeneration is a slow and progressive process, justifying the mixing of young CN with AD patients for estimating AD trajectories. The paper emphasizes clinical applicability and interpretability as key advantages over deep learning methods. Polynomial models were predominantly quadratic, except for inferior lateral ventricle (cubic). Confidence intervals were estimated at 95% level. The paper also tested but did not use the hippocampal-ventricle ratio (HVR), finding it performed 7 percentage points worse than HAVAs for diagnosis. Multi-site data from seven databases were used without explicit harmonization. The ClinicaDL software was used to define groups and apply the same selection criteria for fair comparison with deep learning methods.
